newsitem.title: ITALY: FOCUS - Lower house approves bulk of Italian budget.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Lower house approves bulk of Italian budget.

text.p: The lower house of parliament approved the core of the Italian government's 1997 austerity budget on Friday, a milestone towards the return of the lira to the European Exchange Rate Mechanism (ERM).

The controversial package, which is designed to slice 62.5 trillion lire ($41 billion) off next year's projected public sector deficit, was passed in the early hours of the morning after a marathon parliamentary sitting.

The final two sections of the budget law, which contain overall spending guidelines for various state bodies, are expected to be voted on by Sunday. The bill will then pass to the Senate (upper house) for ratification.
Prime Minister Romano Prodi says the belt-tightening financial package is vital to Italy's hopes of becoming a founder member of Europe's planned single currency.

As a first step towards this goal, the lira must return to the ERM. Prodi has repeatedly said that as soon as the budget passes the turbulent lower chamber he will ask European Union partners to accept the lira back into the ERM fold, four years after it was ejected from the grid during a currency crisis.

"If the lira is not put back in next weekend, it will probably happen the following one," Lorenzo Stanca, head of research at bank Credito Italiano in Milan told Reuters Financial Television. "We think we are almost there."
But any relief in government ranks over the approval of the bulk of the budget has been tempered by the shock resignation of Public Works Minister Antonio Di Pietro.
The former graft-busting magistrate, who enjoys hero status in Italy, quit on Thursday after coming under investigation over alleged malpractice during his time as a prosecutor.

And although Prodi has got the main budgetary measures through the Chamber, where his centre-left coalition depends on support from the hardline Communist Refoundation to govern, he still faces widespread discontent over the package.
The main centre-right opposition parties boycotted the vote on Friday while the unions repeated their threat to call a general strike in protest at the budget.
The leaders of Italy's three largest unions are scheduled to meet Prodi on Monday and are up in arms about a planned fiscal reform which will hurt employees more than self-employed people.
"This is an invitation to consider next Monday's meeting as useless and immediately call a general strike," said Pietro Larizza, head of the Uil union.
The budget is due to go before the full Senate on December 10 and various upper house committees have been asked to express an opinion on the package by November 27.

Political sources said they would have their work cut out studying the confusing mass of measures approved by the lower house, which contain numerous amendments and even old cabinet decrees tagged onto the bill at the last minute.
"There's an enormous amount of technical work to be done in the Senate to try to straighten out the confusion," one parliamentary source said.
But commentators thought the budget's passage would be smooth, as the coalition enjoys a majority in the Senate.
"Theoretically it could have problems but it's fair to say that the main political problems are now past," Credito's Stanca said.
